Title: FAIR_XAI: Improving Multimodal Foundation Model Fairness via Explainability for Wellbeing Assessment
Text:
FAIR_XAI: Improving Multimodal Foundation Model Fairness via
Explainability for Wellbeing Assessment
Sophie Chiang∗†
Tom Brennan∗†
Fethiye Irmak Dogan†
Jiaee Cheong†‡
Hatice Gunes†
Abstract
In recent years, the integration of multimodal machine learning
in wellbeing assessment has offered transformative potential for
monitoring mental health. However, with the rapid advancement
of Vision-Language Models (VLMs), their deployment in clinical
settings has raised concerns due to their lack of transparency and
potential for bias. While previous research has explored the in-
tersection of fairness and Explainable AI (XAI), its application to
VLMs for wellbeing assessment and depression prediction remains
under-explored. This work investigates VLM performance across
laboratory (AFAR-BSFT) and naturalistic (E-DAIC) datasets, focus-
ing on diagnostic reliability and demographic fairness. Performance
varied substantially across environments and architectures; Phi-
3.5-Vision achieved 80.4% accuracy on E-DAIC, while Qwen2-VL
struggled at 33.9%. Additionally, both models demonstrated a ten-
dency to over-predict depression on AFAR-BSFT. Although bias
existed across both architectures, Qwen2-VL showed higher gen-
der disparities, while Phi-3.5-Vision exhibited more racial bias. Our
XAI intervention framework yielded mixed results; fairness prompt-
ing achieved perfect equal opportunity for Qwen2-VL at a severe
accuracy cost on E-DAIC. On AFAR-BSFT, explainability-based
interventions improved procedural consistency but did not guar-
antee outcome fairness, sometimes amplifying racial bias. These
results highlight a persistent gap between procedural transparency
and equitable outcomes. We analyse these findings and consoli-
date concrete recommendations for addressing them, emphasising
that future fairness interventions must jointly optimise predictive
accuracy, demographic parity, and cross-domain generalisation.
Keywords
Vision-Language Models (VLMs), Multimodal Machine Learning,
Human-Robot Interaction, Explainable AI
1
Introduction
Clinical depression remains one of the most prevalent mental health
disorders, affecting approximately 332 million people worldwide,
and is a leading cause of disability [1]. The application of multi-
modal machine learning (ML) to wellbeing assessment has seen
a significant surge in popularity, offering promising methods for
monitoring mental health illnesses and predicting patient outcomes.
More recently, this trend has accelerated further with the adoption
of Multimodal Foundation Models, and, more specifically, Vision-
Language Models (VLMs) [39]. Unlike traditional supervised learn-
ing, VLMs are often pre-trained on large-scale image-text corpora

[23, 58], allowing for zero-shot reasoning and prediction without
explicit re-training [2, 45], opening the door to more scalable and
autonomous clinical solutions.
Despite this potential, the deployment of VLMs in clinical set-
tings is currently bottlenecked by a “black-box" dilemma [46]. In
wellbeing prediction, this lack of transparency can make it diffi-
cult for clinicians to discern whether a classification is based on
valid clinical markers, or a result of ML prediction bias [2, 21], i.e.,
when there is prejudice or favouritism towards an individual or
group based on their inherent or acquired characteristics [42]. Ex-
plainable AI (XAI) has been proposed to bridge this gap between
performance and trust. XAI refers to the suite of ML techniques
that produce more explainable models while maintaining a high
level of performance, and enable humans to understand and effec-
tively manage the emerging generation of artificially intelligent
partners [7]. However, while previous studies have explored the
intersection of fairness and explainability [23, 59], the relationship
for VLMs in wellbeing assessment, and more specifically depression
classification, is significantly under-explored.
This paper therefore investigates the following research ques-
tions: (RQ1) How does zero-shot VLM depression classification
performance vary between controlled laboratory datasets and nat-
uralistic, unconstrained clinical environments? It is important to
understand how VLM performance can vary across different types
of data domains, and to determine how environmental noise and
data distribution shifts impact VLM diagnostic reliability. We also
ask (RQ2): To what extent do systematic performance disparities
(e.g. gender-based accuracy) persist across VLM architectures, and
are these biases consistent across both controlled and naturalistic
data domains? Since we use multiple VLM architectures, we can
evaluate whether any bias that exists is model or domain-specific.
Finally, we ask (RQ3): Can an XAI-guided intervention method be
systematically deployed to improve VLM outcome fairness?
The contributions of this paper are therefore threefold. First,
we provide a cross-domain benchmark demonstrating how zero-
shot VLM performance in depression classification shifts between
naturalistic and laboratory settings. Our findings revealed that
performance varied substantially across environments and archi-
tectures. Second, we present a fairness audit that reveals how and
what biases are model or domain-specific. Finally, we evaluate our
XAI-guided intervention, which yielded mixed results; an increase
in procedural consistency did not always translate to equitable
outcomes, and in some cases, even amplified bias. By document-
ing these results, this paper provides a roadmap for future work,
highlighting the importance of models that must jointly take into
account demographic fairness, predictive performance, and clin-
ical viability across diverse populations. We collate the resulting

2
Related Work
Multimodal Wellbeing Assessment. The integration of multi-
modal data, such as facial, acoustic, and textual features, has become
increasingly standard for computational wellbeing assessment, as
it captures a richer set of human behaviours than traditional uni-
modal approaches [12, 16, 35, 44]. Multimodal data has been used
in various affective computing tasks, such as depression assess-
ment [4, 16, 18, 30] and automated pain detection [8, 29]. Recently,
this field has seen a significant shift from traditional statistical mod-
els to large pre-trained foundation models. Initially, this was led
by Large Language Models (LLMs) for text-based mental health
support [37, 51], which also later spurred the development of con-
versational AI agents [25], as well as the use of social robotics for
stress reduction [36, 50]. Concurrently, VLMs have emerged and
have been noticed for their zero-shot and few-shot capabilities, as
well as their use for such multimodal tasks. For instance, Abbasi et
al. demonstrated the use of a lightweight, open-source VLM in a
robot-led approach for child wellbeing assessment [2]. The model’s
performance also demonstrated a significantly higher false positive
rate for girls, potentially indicating sensitivity to gender attributes.
Fairness in Affective Computing. Bias in affective computing
has been well-documented [10, 13, 15, 20], especially regarding gen-
der [17, 29] and ethnicity [10, 14]. Domnich et al. [24] investigated
gender fairness of ML models in emotion recognition, and Cameron
et al. [10] for pain detection from facial expressions. Lee et al. [38]
not only found performance gaps between gender and ethnicity
groups, but also gender-correlated features that help explain why
this is the case. Recent LLM [51] and VLM [2, 23] studies have
mirrored these concerns. There is also a concern that these models
may exaggerate existing healthcare biases, due to the social preju-
dice already present in training data [31, 53]. While these studies
mainly focus on auditing the existence of bias in model outcomes,
our work aims to extend this by investigating how we can use
XAI-driven insights to actively mitigate these disparities in VLMs
without task-specific fine-tuning.
Explainable AI. Previous research has developed XAI methods
that have been shown to be important in debugging [22, 26, 43],
building trust [54], and diagnosing bias in various prediction tasks [6].
Helbling et al. introduced the idea of a Concept Attention frame-
work, which offers higher-level interpretability, localising textual
concepts within visual data, and producing clear saliency maps to vi-
sualise how a model links semantic prompts to visual elements [33].
While such frameworks have been applied to tasks such as general
image segmentation, our work aims to apply such interpretability
principles to the more subjective and nuanced domain of wellbeing
assessment. Recent studies have started to explore the intersec-
tion of fairness and explainability. For example, Lundberg et al.
demonstrated how model disparity can be decomposed into feature-
specific contributions, in order to locate the source of bias [40].
Furthermore, Zhao et al. [59] presented a set of metrics (Ratio and
Value-based Explanation Fairness) in order to mitigate procedure-
based bias, in addition to a Comprehensive Fairness Algorithm that
improved traditional fairness, satisfied explanation fairness and
maintained utility performance. Despite these advancements, the
intersection between fairness and explainability remains under-
explored for large-scale VLMs in affective computing.
3
Methodology
The overall pipeline is illustrated in Figure 1. First, we have per-
modality feature extraction from raw audio, visual and verbal sig-
nals. Second, two parallel classification pathways, a zero-shot gener-
ative pipeline in which the VLM is prompted directly and an embed-
ding-based fusion pipeline in which frozen VLM text encodings are
combined with audio and facial MLP encodings. Third, XAI-guided
interventions via prompt-based chain-of-thought and fairness rule
set for the generative pathway and a counterfactual fairness loss for
the embedding pathway. Fourth, a joint explainability-and-fairness
audit that scores reasoning quality (Δ𝑅𝐸𝐹) alongside outcome fair-
ness (Δ𝐸𝑂, disparate impact, accuracy gaps).

3.3
Embedding Classification Pipeline
As an alternative to the generative classification pipeline, we intro-
duce the embedding-based pipeline that extracts fixed-dimensional
representations from frozen VLM encoders and trains a lightweight
fusion classifier on top. This approach enables systematic ablation
studies across modality combinations while amortising the com-
putational cost of VLM inference. By making our fusion classifier
highly configurable, we compare performance across all combina-
tions of text, audio and facial modalities; for each, we extract a
fixed-dimensional embedding:
• Text: We take interview transcripts through the VLM’s text
encoder and extract the final hidden state representation. For
a given backbone model, e.g., Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct (hidden
size 1536) and Phi-3.5-Vision-Instruct (hidden size 3072), we
applied a linear projection to 256 dimensions.
• Audio: OpenSMILE eGeMAPS features were processed by a
3-layer MLP to a 128-dimensional embedding.
• Facial: OpenFace 2.0 features were encoded via a 3-layer
MLP to a 128-dimensional embedding.
Modality embeddings were then concatenated via early fusion:
hfused = [htext; haudio; hfacial] ∈R512 (from our 256 + 128 + 128 di-
mensions). This fused representation is then given to a 2-layer
classification head: R512

logits for binary classification. The fusion classifier and modal-
ity encoders (audio/facial MLPs) were trained end-to-end using
cross-entropy loss with class weights to deal with the dataset’s
depressed/non-depressed class imbalance.
3.4
Intervention Framework
3.4.1
Prompt-Based Fairness Intervention. For the generative clas-
sification pipeline (Section 3.2), we use a lightweight prompt-based
intervention that combines chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning with
explicit fairness instructions. Rather than modifying the data or
retraining the model, we append two extra components to the task
instruction T at inference time: a chain-of-thought reasoning di-
rective and a fairness rule set.
For the reasoning directive, the VLM is asked to produce its
reasoning in a <thinking> block before outputting its final label
in a <classification> block (“Depressed” or “Not Depressed”).
This encourages the model to ground its prediction in the clinical
biomarkers in B𝑖, and also gives us a reasoning trace that we can
later score with the Δ𝑅𝐸𝐹audit. For the fairness rule set, we append
a short set of instructions that tell the model to base its assessment
only on clinical indicators, ignore demographic factors such as
gender and race, apply consistent standards across groups, and
self-correct if it notices itself making demographic assumptions.
3.4.2
Counterfactual Fairness Algorithm (CFA). For the embedding-
classification pipeline (Section 3.3), we made a training-time inter-
vention to identify and penalise features that contribute to biased
predictions, inspired by the framework used by Zhao et al. [59].
We achieve this by computing gradient-based feature attributions
using integrated gradients [52] for each feature during training. If a
feature has high importance for the prediction but is also strongly

We modify the loss function to include this fairness penalty:

4
Experiments
4.1
Datasets
We use two datasets; both datasets are in English and cover similar
wellbeing contexts and are described below.
AFAR-BSFT Dataset consists of 44 weekly 20-minute sessions
from 11 participants [19], where data was recorded in a dyadic
setting with a well-being coach. Extracted features include 709
facial features (Action Units, gaze, pose), 172 audio features, and
two verbal biomarkers (label and probability).
E-DAIC Dataset contains 275 semi-clinical interviews [47]. It in-
cluded 73 hours of interviews, with the ground truth label being
PHQ-8 scores. Features comprise 17 facial Action Units via Open-
Face, acoustic descriptors (pitch, loudness, voice jitter) and auto-
matic text transcriptions.
The two datasets required different preprocessing because they are
distributed differently. For AFAR-BSFT, the audio, visual and ver-
bal biomarkers were supplied as separate per-session tables. These
were merged into a single per-session multimodal feature vector by
joining on the session filename column, which uniquely identifies a
participant–session pair. In addition, sessions with missing values
were removed. For E-DAIC, each participant directory contained
modality-specific files keyed by participant ID rather than a shared
filename. Frame-level audio and facial streams were collapsed to a
single per-session vector by concatenating five summary statistics
(mean, standard deviation, minimum, maximum, median) over each
channel. Missing or invalid entries within a frame were imputed
to zero rather than removed, and a participant was excluded only
when an entire modality file was missing.
4.2
Model Selection
We evaluate two state-of-the-art, small-scale VLMs that are suitable
for resource-constrained environments (Google Colab T4 GPU).
The first is Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct, a 2 billion parameter model that
introduces Naive Dynamic Resolution and Multimodal Rotary Posi-
tion Embedding to enhance image and visual understanding that
aligns closely with human perceptual processes [55]. The second
is Microsoft’s Phi-3.5-Vision-Instruct, a 4.2 billion parameter model
that is lightweight and built upon datasets that include high-quality
synthetic data and filtered publicly available websites, ensuring
reasoning-dense data across text and vision [3]. We prioritised mod-
els that are relevant, feasible, and have shown strong performance
on related multimodal tasks.

4.3.1
Fairness Measures. Let 𝐴∈{0, 1} be a sensitive attribute,
where 𝐴= 1 represents the majority group and 𝐴= 0 represents
the minority or protected group. For example, in the AFAR-BSFT
dataset, 𝐴𝑟𝑎𝑐𝑒= 1 if the participant is white and 𝐴𝑟𝑎𝑐𝑒= 0 if they
are not white. We evaluate the models using the following metrics,
similar to existing works [57]:
• Equal Accuracy (EA), a group-based metric, can be calcu-
lated to compare group fairness between models. In other
words, it is the absolute difference in classification accuracy
between the majority and minority groups, where a high
gap can indicate that the model is better calibrated for the
majority group [57].
𝐸𝐴= |𝑃( ˆ𝑦= 𝑦|𝐴= 1) −𝑃( ˆ𝑦= 𝑦|𝐴= 0)|
• Equal opportunity (EO), measures the true positive rate
across all groups. Low true positive rates for an under-represented
group could have serious consequences for diagnosis and

𝐸𝑂= |𝑃( ˆ𝑦= 1|𝑦= 1,𝐴= 1) −𝑃( ˆ𝑦= 1|𝑦= 1,𝐴= 0)|
• Disparate impact (DI), measures whether positive out-
comes occur at similar rates across groups, flagging where
systems may not recognise positive outcomes for certain
minority groups [27]:
𝐷𝐼= 𝑃( ˆ𝑦= 1|𝐴= 0)

4.3.2
Explainability Measures. REF is a result-oriented metric and
serves as a diagnostic tool to evaluate the consistency of a model’s
underlying logic [59]. It measures the disparity in Explanation
Quality (EQ) between a minority group (𝑠= 0) and a majority
group (𝑠= 1):
Δ𝑅𝐸𝐹= |𝑃( ˆ𝑞= 1|𝑠= 0) −𝑃( ˆ𝑞= 1|𝑠= 1)|
where ˆ𝑞is the quality label for the explanation. An explanation is
labelled as high-quality (ˆ𝑞= 1) if the VLM successfully grounds its
prediction in specific, valid clinical biomarkers provided in the
prompt. Otherwise, an explanation that is labelled low-quality
(ˆ𝑞= 0), exhibits “hallucinated" rationales, relying on demographic
proxies, or produces inconsistent reasoning that contradicts pro-
vided feature data. The metric Δ𝑅𝐸𝐹measures the unfairness of
high-quality proportion for subgroups, where a smaller value re-
lates to a fairer model [59].

4.4
RQ1 Experiments: Zero-shot performance
To evaluate how zero-shot VLM performance varies between con-
trolled and naturalistic environments, we deploy the generative
classification pipeline, as explained in Section 3.2, across both the
AFAR-BSFT and E-DAIC datasets. We calculate and report standard
classification metrics, including accuracy, F1-Score, precision and
recall for both VLM models and datasets.
4.5
RQ2 Experiments: Performance disparities
To investigate the extent of performance disparities across VLM
architectures, we report fairness audit metrics, including Equal Ac-
curacy (EA), Equal Opportunity (EO) and Disparate Impact (DI).
Additionally, we deploy the embedding-based classification pipeline,
as explained in Section 3.3, on the E-DAIC dataset to perform a
modality ablation suite, due to the raw modality data available. We
evaluate seven different configurations by extracting embeddings
from the frozen VLM, ranging from unimodal (text, audio or fa-
cial only) to full-fusion, so we can observe how different modality
signals may impact bias and performance.
4.6
RQ3 Experiments: XAI-guided interventions
To evaluate our XAI-guided intervention framework, we deploy our
instructive fairness prompting strategy to the generative pipeline
on both datasets, explicitly directing the VLMs to mitigate demo-
graphic bias, such as race and gender. On the E-DAIC dataset, we
implement the Counterfactual Fairness Algorithm (CFA) within the
embedding pipeline, using integrated gradients for feature attri-
bution during training. Post-intervention, we recalculate all per-
formance and fairness metrics and report Ratio-based Explanation
Fairness (Δ𝑅𝐸𝐹) across both datasets and VLM architectures to
determine if these intervention strategies improve procedural con-
sistency and reasoning quality across demographic subgroups.

BSFT) and naturalistic (E-DAIC) domains revealed significant archi-
tectural discrepancies (Table 1, “Classification Performance” rows).
On the AFAR-BSFT dataset, Qwen2-VL achieved a raw baseline

yielded an accuracy of 0.561 and an F1-score of 0.667. Additionally,
Qwen2-VL displayed a Cohen’s Kappa score of 𝜅= 0.020, while
Phi-3.5-Vision was 𝜅= 0.047. Of these, Qwen2-VL produced 16
false positives (1 false negative) and Phi-3.5-Vision produced 12

E-DAIC, under the zero-shot generative pipeline, Phi-3.5-Vision
achieved 0.786 accuracy on text-only and improved to 0.804 in
the full-fusion configuration. In contrast, Qwen2-VL achieved only
0.482 accuracy on text-only, with full-fusion degrading performance

6
Discussion
RQ1: How does zero-shot VLM depression classification per-
formance vary between controlled laboratory datasets and
naturalistic clinical environments?
From our results, both VLM models demonstrate that in con-
trolled laboratory environments (AFAR-BSFT), there is a tendency
towards high sensitivity at the expense of specificity. The high false-
positive counts reported suggest that in the absence of fine-tuning,
these baseline zero-shot models default to a conservative screening
posture, prioritising the capture of depressive cues backed by high
recall, even when cues may not indicate as such [31, 34]. From a
clinical perspective, a high False Positive Rate (FPR) is often deemed
to be better and more acceptable than a high False Negative Rate
(FNR), especially in a mental health screening, as it ensures vul-
nerable individuals are not overlooked [41]. However, Qwen2-VL’s
tendency to predict the positive class as a safe default indicated a
lack of nuanced diagnostic thresholds. While this results in high

Furthermore, while the accuracy of 0.585 and 0.561 for Qwen2-VL
and Phi-3.5-Vision represents our baseline capability of zero-shot
reasoning, they remain notably inferior to state-of-the art multi-
modal models. Traditional machine learning approaches, such as
those discussed in [10], utilise domain-specific training to miti-
gate the environmental noise and over-sensitivity present in our
zero-shot inference setup.
(RQ2): To what extent do systematic performance dispari-
ties (e.g. gender-based accuracy) persist across different VLM
architectures, and are these biases consistent across both
controlled and naturalistic data domains?
The facial action units, verbal features and physical dynamics
that we use in these audits are highly sensitive biometric data;
the analysis below should be understood as taking place within
a strictly research-bounded use of that data. For the controlled
laboratory dataset (AFAR-BSFT), our analysis on baseline dispari-
ties indicates that demographic bias is present across both tested
architectures, though the nature of bias varies between models.
The AFAR-BSFT fairness audit (Section 5, Table 1; Figure 4) shows
Qwen2-VL’s bias profile is gender-dominated while Phi-3.5-Vision’s
is race-dominated with the latter showing an equal opportunity gap
roughly four times its gender equivalent. We interpret this diver-
gence as architecture-specific: in the smaller Qwen2-VL, gendered
facial cues appear to act as a stronger proxy for diagnostic decisions,
whereas Phi-3.5-Vision is more prone to representation bias along
racial lines, perhaps inherited from its training distribution.
On the E-DAIC dataset, bias values were heavily shaped by the
chosen fusion strategy and classification paradigm. The generative
approach had very different fairness characteristics compared to
embedding-based classification. The cross-paradigm comparison re-
ported in Section 5 suggests that the generative pipeline is markedly

further note that adding multimodal signals dilutes text-specific
bias under both paradigms, although the embedding approach has
higher overall bias. A possible explanation for the dilution effect we
have when adding more modalities is that text encoders in VLMs
encode demographic proxies, like gendered language or dialect
features, that can cause bias in the model and are spuriously cor-
related with the sensitive attribute [9, 56]. When audio and facial
streams are incorporated, the fused representation is forced to inte-
grate evidence from modalities that carry different, complementary
diagnostic signals [44]. This cross-modal integration reduces the
model’s over-reliance on any single biased channel by increasing
the feature dimensionality and distributing representational weight
across sources, and this effect was supported by audio-visual fusion
systems exhibiting significantly lower demographic disparity than
their unimodal counterparts [28].
The ablation suite revealed that certain modality combinations
dramatically amplify bias rather than averaging it out. For Qwen2-
VL, the text and facial configuration achieved Δ𝐸𝑂= 0.418 (Fig-
ure 2), the highest observed bias across all experiments, almost 3
times higher than the text only configuration (Δ𝐸𝑂= 0.153), and
much higher than full fusion (Δ𝐸𝑂= 0.306).
(RQ3): Can an XAI-guided intervention method be systemat-
ically deployed to improve VLM outcome fairness?
In the controlled laboratory dataset (AFAR-BSFT), the interven-
tion yielded a notable improvement in the diagnostic quality of
Qwen2-VL: Cohen’s𝜅rose substantially and Δ𝑅𝐸𝐹decreased across
7


all demographic subgroups (Figure 4), indicating more logically con-
sistent and procedurally fair reasoning. The technical improvement
nevertheless reveals a paradox: improved procedural logic does not
guarantee improved outcome fairness. The model’s gender accuracy
gap shrank but its opportunity difference and disparate impact ratio
worsened, and racial bias was substantially amplified. We interpret
this as evidence that forcing a model to ground its explanations
may anchor it more firmly to biased internal representations of
specific biomarkers, with XAI acting here as a diagnostic window
into existing prejudices rather than as a corrective.
The impact on Phi-3.5-Vision presents a contrasting narrative:
post-intervention, predictive validity collapses (Cohen’s 𝜅becomes
negative; see Figure 3), and although racial fairness metrics improve
dramatically, the simultaneous reduction in Δ𝑅𝐸𝐹must be inter-
preted with caution. When fairness gains coincide with sub-random
performance, it is plausible that parity is achieved through random
noise rather than equitable reasoning. Such a result is functionally
hollow and clinically unviable. This finding underscores a broader
ethical concern: explanations from VLMs derive their value from
factual truthfulness, not surface plausibility.

Conclusion
Our findings reveal key insights. First, zero-shot VLM performance
varies substantially across environments and architectures. Phi-3.5-
Vision had strong generative classification performance on the E-
DAIC dataset (80.4%), while Qwen2-VL struggled with the same task
(33.9%). In addition, both models demonstrated a tendency to over-
predict depression labels for the AFAR-BSFT dataset, showcasing
fairly conservative screening assessments. Secondly, demographic
bias was present across both VLM architectures. Qwen2-VL showed
higher gender-based disparities, whereas Phi-3.5-Vision had more
racial bias. Thirdly, our guided XAI intervention framework pro-
duced mixed results. On E-DAIC, fairness prompting achieved per-
fect equal opportunity for Qwen2-VL at a severe accuracy cost. On
AFAR-BSFT interventions improved procedural consistency but
did not guarantee fairer outcomes, in some cases amplifying racial
bias. Further work could explore additional datasets and models
for more robust benchmarking. In addition, training or fine-tuning
a VLM that is domain invariant and able to recognise biomarkers
despite the environmental setting might improve generalisability.
To further improve prediction bias, future work could explore how
VLM adversarial training may affect model behaviour and whether
a secondary independent model that judges whether rationales are
demographically biased improves overall performance. Drawing
these threads together, Table 3 consolidates our findings into ac-
tionable recommendations for the responsible deployment of VLMs
in clinical wellbeing assessment, organised by research question.

automation bias, where high-quality explanations or hallucinations
might lead clinicians to overlook subtle diagnostic nuances or even

Abstract: In recent years, the integration of multimodal machine learning in wellbeing assessment has offered transformative potential for monitoring mental health. However, with the rapid advancement of Vision-Language Models (VLMs), their deployment in clinical settings has raised concerns due to their lack of transparency and potential for bias. While previous research has explored the in- tersection of fairness and Explainable AI (XAI), its application to VLMs for wellbeing assessment and depression prediction remains under-explored. This work investigates VLM performance across laboratory (AFAR-BSFT) and naturalistic (E-DAIC) datasets, focus- ing on diagnostic reliability and demographic fairness. Performance varied substantially across environments and architectures; Phi- 3.5-Vision achieved 80.4% accuracy on E-DAIC, while Qwen2-VL struggled at 33.9%. Additionally, both models demonstrated a ten- dency to over-predict depression on AFAR-BSFT. Although bias existed across both architectures, Qwen2-VL showed higher gen- der disparities, while Phi-3.5-Vision exhibited more racial bias. Our XAI intervention framework yielded mixed results; fairness prompt- ing achieved perfect equal opportunity for Qwen2-VL at a severe accuracy cost on E-DAIC. On AFAR-BSFT, explainability-based interventions improved procedural consistency but did not guar- antee outcome fairness, sometimes amplifying racial bias. These results highlight a persistent gap between procedural transparency and equitable outcomes. We analyse these findings and consoli- date concrete recommendations for addressing them, emphasising that future fairness interventions must jointly optimise predictive accuracy, demographic parity, and cross-domain generalisation.
